items.titel: Russia complains of ‘new Iron Curtain’ as Estonia shuts its borders
items.anriss: Tallinn's decision to shut road border crossings comes after an attack on a drone manufacturer.

absaetze.t: Tallinn’s decision to shut road border crossings comes after an attack on a drone manufacturer.

Moscow has accused Estonia of planning to build a “new Iron Curtain”, and promised to respond, after the small Baltic nation formally decided to close all border crossings with Russia to the east and south.
Estonia’s government on Friday approved a preliminary six-month closure of its road border crossings from December 1, and will decide next year whether to extend it.

Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Maria Zakharova told a news briefing in Moscow that “should Tallinn proceed with these plans, our country will take the necessary political and diplomatic measures in response to safeguard its national interests.”
“Such moves are tantamount to attempts to erect a new Iron Curtain under the false pretence of some sort of threat from the East,” Zakharova added.
In Tallinn on Friday, Estonia’s Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna described the border closure as “an important measure”.
“It will reduce opportunities to exploit cross-border movement to recruit people, conduct influence operations, organise acts of sabotage or circumvent sanctions,” he said.

Estonia, a NATO and EU member and a staunch supporter of Ukraine, first announced the border closure earlier this month, accusing Russia of being behind an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.
The Kremlin denied the accusation at the time, saying it was part of what it called a pattern of false allegations levelled against Moscow by European countries.
Estonia’s northern neighbour Finland shut its Russia border crossings in 2023, and has kept them closed since then, while southern Baltic nations ⁠Latvia and Lithuania maintain open crossings.
Of the 760,000 people who crossed the Estonia-Russia border this year, 307,000 were Russian nationals, 175,000 were Estonian citizens and 54,000 held Finnish passports, Estonian ‌police ‌data showed.
Rail freight is not affected by the road closure, but remains subject to strict customs checks, Estonia said.

items.titel: Großbritannien: Schuldsprüche in Vergewaltigungsprozess
items.anriss: Der Fall erinnert an das Martyrium der Französin Gisèle Pelicot. Die Britin Joanne Young wurde über Jahre von ihrem Ehemann betäubt - und dann im Internet zur Vergewaltigung angeboten. Nun wurden vier Männer schuldig gesprochen. Von F. …

absaetze.t: Ehefrau betäubt und im Internet angeboten Schuldsprüche in britischem Vergewaltigungsprozess

Der Fall erinnert an das Martyrium der Französin Gisèle Pelicot. Die Britin Joanne Young wurde über Jahre von ihrem Ehemann betäubt - und dann im Internet zur Vergewaltigung angeboten. Nun wurden vier Männer schuldig gesprochen.

Joanne Young tritt gefasst vor die Kameras vor dem Strafgericht in Winchester - sie hat bewusst auf ihr Recht auf Anonymität verzichtet. Denn ihr Name und Gesicht sollen anderen Frauen Mut machen. Das gerade verkündete Urteil gebe ihr Hoffnung, sagt sie.

"Es bedeutet, dass sich Betroffene in einer ähnlichen Situation wie ich eher zu Wort melden werden, eher Vertrauen in das Strafrechtssystem haben werden. Es vermittelt Frauen und Mädchen die Botschaft, dass man ihnen Glauben schenkt und sie versteht."
Young war immer wieder von ihrem damaligen Ehemann betäubt worden. Er mischte Medikamente in ihre Getränke. Dann lud er fremde Männer ein, sie sexuell zu missbrauchen. Mehr als 13 Jahre lang.
Erstmals auch Mittäter verurteilt

"Die Person, der ich am meisten vertraut habe, hat mich auf schrecklichste Weise betrogen. Das hatte verheerende Auswirkungen auf mein Leben und das meiner Kinder. Aber es war nicht die Tat eines Einzelnen. Andere haben sich entschieden, mitzumachen und sich dadurch mitschuldig gemacht. Und das heutige Urteil trägt dem Rechnung", sagt Young nach der Verkündung des Urteils.

Youngs Ex-Mann hatte sich bereits schuldig bekannt in 56 Anklagepunkten, darunter elf Fälle von Vergewaltigung, und wartet jetzt auf seine Strafe. Nun hat eine Jury vier weitere Männer schuldig gesprochen. Es ist das erste Mal, dass in England mehrere Angeklagte gemeinsam wegen organisierter, durch Drogen ermöglichter sexueller Übergriffe verurteilt wurden.

Die britische Staatsanwaltschaft erklärte in einer Pressemitteilung: Sie registriere eine steigende Zahl solcher Fälle und arbeite mit den Ermittlungsbehörden zusammen, um weitere Täter vor Gericht zu bringen.
Keine Folgen für Tech-Konzerne

Angeboten hatte Philip Young seine Ehefrau auf Anzeigenportalen im Internet. Das widerfuhr auch der Britin Laura Bishop. Ihr Ehemann war bereits 2022 verurteilt worden, wie sie im BBC Radio berichtet: "Die Webseiten, auf denen mein Mann mich anderen Männern angeboten hat, sind nach wie vor online. Der Polizei ist bekannt, dass sie keine Beweismittel oder forensischen Daten zur Verfügung stellen. Forscher wissen, dass dort Sexualstraftäter unterwegs sind. Warum sind sie also in Großbritannien immer noch zugänglich? Das muss aufhören."

Miranda Horvath, Direktorin des Instituts für soziale Gerechtigkeit und Kriminalität an der University of Suffolk, fordert ein konsequenteres Vorgehen der Politik gegen die Tech-Unternehmen. "Es geht darum, die Tech-Unternehmen und Plattformen zur Rechenschaft zu ziehen, die dieses Material weiterhin verbreiten, und zu sagen: 'Das reicht, wir tolerieren so etwas in unserer Gesellschaft nicht.' Sie verdienen viel Geld mit dem Leid und dem Schmerz anderer Menschen."
Täter kommen aus allen Schichten

Die Männer, die auf diesen Seiten und Apps unterwegs sind, hätten oft völlig unterschiedliche Hintergründe, ergänzt die Wissenschaftlerin. "Diese Straftaten werden selten angezeigt und selten aufgedeckt, aber wir wissen, dass es sich um Männer aus allen Gesellschaftsschichten handelt, die dem Opfer in der Regel bekannt sind. Sie nutzen Gelegenheiten, die sich ihnen bieten, schaffen Gelegenheiten und nutzen das Vertrauen und die Verbundenheit in langfristigen Beziehungen aus."
Sexualstraftäter Young war Kommunalpolitiker und Unternehmer. Einer der anderen Männer arbeitete an Projekten zur nuklearen Verteidigung des Verteidigungsministeriums mit.
Joanne Young sagte nach dem Urteil: Sie sei fest entschlossen, sich nicht durch die Taten der Männer definieren zu lassen. Sie wolle nun anderen Opfern helfen.
Die Strafe für die Täter soll Ende Dezember verkündet werden.

items.titel: Israeli drone attacks kill seven Palestinians in central Gaza
items.anriss: Drones cause 'fear and panic' among Palestinians as Israel continues attacks on the Strip despite 'ceasefire'.

absaetze.t: Buzzing of drones causes ‘fear and panic’ among Palestinians as Israel continues attacks on the Strip despite ‘ceasefire’.
Israeli attacks have killed at least seven Palestinians and wounded others in the central part of the Gaza Strip, as attacks continue despite a “ceasefire” agreement.
Four Palestinians were killed on Friday when an Israeli drone struck the Bureij refugee camp in Deir el-Balah, medical sources told Al Jazeera.
Witnesses said the drone targeted a group of civilians within the camp.
Separately, a medical source at al-Awda Hospital reported the arrival of the body of a Palestinian killed by an Israeli drone strike in the Nuseirat refugee camp.
Two Palestinians were also killed when an Israeli drone struck civilians near the entrance to the city of Deir el-Balah.
Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud, reporting from Deir el-Balah, said the injured were brought to hospitals in central Gaza that operate at reduced capacity due to a lack of medical supplies and staff.
Mahmoud added that drones were “causing fear and panic” among Palestinians in Gaza.
“People cannot run simple errands because of the ongoing fear of being attacked and killed on the road,” he said.
The buzzing of drones adds to the sound of explosions from home demolitions and to that of fighter jets, our correspondent added.
The Israeli army on Friday carried out demolition operations near areas under its control in the al-Shuja’iya neighbourhood in the eastern part of Gaza City using explosive-laden drones.
It also carried out three large-scale demolitions near the “Yellow Line”, east of Khan Younis in southern Gaza.
By June 16, 2026, an estimated 201,290 structures in Gaza had been damaged or destroyed, about 82 percent of all structures in the Strip, according to the United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT).
Israeli forces have continued demolishing buildings and homes in the Gaza Strip amid ongoing military operations and disputes over the “ceasefire” line.
Israel has repeatedly violated the so-called “ceasefire” agreement that entered into force on October 10, 2025.

Since then, Israeli attacks have killed more than 1,600 Palestinians in Gaza. Since the genocidal war began in October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured 176,000 others.

Separately on Friday, which marks World Children’s Day, Palestinian prisoner groups said that around 350 Palestinian children were being held in Israeli prisons, where they face torture, starvation and deprivation of medical care, education, and family visits.

The Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs and the Palestinian Prisoner Society said dozens of children from Gaza were detained during the war, but enforced disappearance and restrictions on visits have made it impossible to determine their numbers.

items.titel: This counter-UAS system senses deep inside neighboring borders to detect and defeat drones
items.anriss: [Sponsored] Long-range detection capabilities extend decision time for counter-UAS actions.

absaetze.t: Drone threats give defenders less time to determine intent and select the appropriate response to protect borders, military installations, and critical infrastructure with no/low collateral damage.

CACI International’s SkyValor next generation drone defense system is designed to expand that decision space through long-range detection and a layered architecture that combines radio frequency (RF) sensing, radar, electronic warfare, cellular detection, and electro-optical and infrared sensors. Breaking Defense talked about SkyValor with CACI’s CTO Jason Bales.
Breaking Defense: Before we get into the details of SkyValor, what threat scenarios is it designed to address, and why are these concerns more urgent now?

Bales: SkyValor builds on more than two decades of designing and deploying counter‑UAS systems worldwide. Over 300 fielded systems have informed our understanding of how drone threats evolve across national security missions, homeland defense, and critical infrastructure protection.

We’ve taken that day‑to‑day operational insight and transformed it into a commercial offering purpose‑built for homeland and national security missions. Border defense is a major focus—tracking drones operating near or across national boundaries, as well as protecting critical infrastructure from incursions. Our long‑range detection gives operators the decision space to determine intent and escalate force appropriately across a rapidly shifting threat landscape.
Range is one of SkyValor’s attributes. Tell us about this.

SkyValor doesn’t just extend the detection envelope, it transforms the entire decision space. While most Group 1–3 systems spot a drone only one to five kilometers out, giving operators a frantic 10‑second window to react, SkyValor reaches an impressive 75 kilometers. That jump in range turns split‑second choices into a deliberate, 18‑ to 20‑minute tactical advantage, giving operators the breathing room to read intent, weigh options, and apply precisely the right level of force.
Describe SkyValor and its components, and where it fits within a broader counter-UAS architecture.

It’s a multi‑layered architecture built for a fast‑moving threat. Our RF heritage enables long‑range detection, signal analysis, and the ability to break into a drone’s communications and create cyber effects—and to apply those effects to steer or take over the platform. The system can also jam broadly when confronting swarms. Our RF and EW capabilities are built in‑house, and we integrate commercial radar for added range and precision. A key differentiator is our cellular‑network technology, which detects and mitigates drones using cellular links, alongside EO/IR sensors and integration with kinetic interceptors.
Tell us about your non-kinetic defeat options.

Non‑kinetic effects allow us to neutralize a drone with almost surgical precision. Instead of relying on expensive interceptors that may require multiple shots, we use software‑driven energy effects that deliver low or no collateral damage and provide an essentially unlimited magazine. It’s the difference between having to physically remove a threat and being able to outthink it by using the system’s intelligence to quietly and efficiently disable or redirect a platform long before it becomes a problem. Kinetic tools certainly have their place, but SkyValor’s long‑range detection lets operators be deliberate rather than reactive. When you have minutes instead of seconds, you can choose the right level of force instead of defaulting to the most aggressive one. That measured escalation preserves valuable interceptors for situations where they’re truly needed.
How does being software-defined change the equation?

Being software‑defined changes the entire equation. It means our non‑kinetic effects aren’t fixed – they evolve. At a recent event, a drone operator tried [JB1] to slip past us by altering their waveform. In half an hour, we pushed a new update across the system and reasserted control. That agility is a hallmark of SkyValor: rather than chasing the threat, we stay ahead of it. The platform adapts in real time, letting operators counter new behaviors as soon as they appear.
What did the recent testing of SkyValor at Yuma and the southern border demonstrate?

Our recent work with JIATF-401 at Yuma and along the southern border was a real proving ground. It combined controlled test runs with unpredictable, real‑world encounters—short‑range pop‑ups, long‑range crossings, low‑altitude skimmers, and drones using a mix of communication links. Every time the environment changed, SkyValor kept pace. Those trials didn’t just validate performance metrics; they demonstrated the system’s ability to adapt to a living, evolving threat landscape.
What does CACI uniquely contribute in detection, tracking, processing, and non-kinetic defeat?

We designed SkyValor to operate autonomously from day one. That means it can collect, detect, track, and relay information without waiting for human intervention—all while feeding curated, AI‑filtered insights back to operators. The autonomy isn’t about removing humans from the equation; it’s about giving them cleaner, more actionable intelligence. When the system is doing the heavy lifting behind the scenes, operators can focus on making confident, well‑timed decisions in a compressed battlespace.
What real-world scenarios best illustrate where SkyValor adds the most value?

Border protection is a prime example. You want to know when a drone is approaching long before it crosses the line, and SkyValor gives you that early warning, turning a few frantic seconds into a structured decision window. In high‑density conflict zones, where threats evolve nightly and new drone behaviors emerge constantly, the system’s software‑defined nature gives operators an advantage: real‑time updates, remote adjustability, and layered sensing that keeps pace with the fight. And when it comes to critical infrastructure like power plants, data centers, and other assets central to national resilience, SkyValor provides the persistent coverage needed to keep mission‑critical sites secure.
What should readers take away about SkyValor?

SkyValor is the culmination of two decades spent tackling the drone problem in the real world. It’s field‑proven, adaptable, and built for missions where speed, scale, and flexibility matter most. Because of our extensive C-UAS knowledge, we successfully moved from concept to deployment in 12 months. Now, as we have moved into full‑rate production, customers are getting more than just a product, they’re getting a foundation for modern layered defense – one that can grow, shift, and respond as fast as the threat itself.

items.titel: Navy CCA Plans Will Not Wait For F/A-XX Next Generation Fighter
items.anriss: One of the key roles envisioned for the U.S. Navy’s next-generation F/A-XX carrier-based fighter is serving as an airborne controller for advanced unmanned aircraft. However, the senior official currently performing the duties of Under …

absaetze.t: One of the key roles envisioned for the U.S. Navy’s next-generation F/A-XX carrier-based fighter is serving as an airborne controller for advanced unmanned aircraft. However, the senior official currently performing the duties of Under Secretary of the Navy says the service does not need to wait for F/A-XX to begin adding Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) type drones to its carrier air wings. The service could pair CCAs first with its F-35C Joint Strike Fighters.

William Toti was asked about the Navy’s CCA plans and their relationship to F/A-XX at a hearing before the Senate Armed Services Committee yesterday. Senators are currently considering Toti’s nomination to formally assume the role of Under Secretary of the Navy.

“CCA aircraft are an element of the future air fleet, the future combat capability of our aircraft carriers. We have been, for better – to put it in a better way, the Air Force has been leading this issue,” Toti said in response to a question from Senator Ted Budd, a North Carolina Republican. “We are following closely behind, but the integration of CCA aircraft in the Air Wing is critically important as we go forward.”

“We need low-cost, attritable assets in our Air Wing, and CCA will provide that. So we have programs in place to begin developing that capability. They’re still nascent,” he continued. “But I see that, with the realignment of the unmanned capability [portfolios] to the [Navy] Under Secretary’s office, which I executed while I was performing the duties of the Under Secretary, I think we’ll get adequate visibility into these issues as we go forward.”

To provide some quick context, in September 2025, the Navy announced it had hired Anduril, Boeing, General Atomics, and Northrop Grumman to develop conceptual designs for future carrier-based CCAs. Lockheed Martin has also been working to develop the underlying control architectures. The Navy’s first fixed-wing carrier-based drone is currently set to be the MQ-25 Stingray, an uncrewed aerial refueling platform.

Just this past September, Boeing also beat out Northrop Grumman to win the F/A-XX competition. Boeing is the prime contractor behind the Air Force’s new F-47 sixth-generation fighter, as well. The Pentagon had previously moved to put F/A-XX on hold indefinitely over concerns about competition for resources with F-47, but Congress subsequently intervened to keep the Navy’s program going.
“Do you think CCA needs to wait on F/A-XX, or do you think that’s something that we can use with current aircraft?” Senator Budd asked Toti yesterday in a follow-up question.

“No, Senator, I think that they’re independent. I think we could probably start integrating systems before F/A-XX delivers,” Toti responded. “Having said that, F/A-XX is a critical capability. We’re going to have these aircraft carriers around for the next 50 years, and the notion that the F-35 is the last airplane that’s going to be launched from them is just a non-starter. “
“We need F/A-XX, and CCA will certainly be probably built into it from [the] ground up, but I think it’s a capability we’ll be able to use with the F-35, specifically, as well,” he added.

“Fifth-generation aircraft, upgraded legacy platforms, and future sixth-generation capabilities each provide distinct operational advantages, while unmanned aircraft offer opportunities to extend operational reach, increase capacity, and complement manned aviation,” Toti also wrote in his prepared responses to policy questions provided in advance of the hearing. “The appropriate mix must preserve near-term readiness while delivering the capabilities necessary to maintain future air dominance.”

It should be noted here that the Air Force currently expects its F-22 Raptors to be its first aerial ‘quarterbacks’ for its forthcoming CCAs. Other platforms, including the F-35 and the F-47, are expected to follow. The Marine Corps is separately planning to pair its first CCAs with F-35s. Lockheed Martin, the prime contractor for the F-22 and the F-35, has been working to lay the groundwork for both platforms to serve in the airborne drone controller role.

Though Toti did not explicitly mention it, Navy CCAs could be teamed up with F/A-18E/F Super Hornet fighters and/or EA-18G Growler electronic warfare jets, too. F/A-XX is slated to eventually replace those aircraft, but not for many more years. TWZ has previously laid out how CCAs could be particularly valuable when paired with fourth-generation tactical jets, also including Air Force F-16s.

The Navy and the Air Force, as well as the Marines, also have a formal agreement in place to use the same or at least compatible control architectures for CCA drones. This is intended to allow for crewed platforms across the services to direct each other’s drones during future operations.

As Toti mentioned, the Navy is still very much in the stages of executing its CCA plans, and not just when it comes to airborne control architectures. Senior officials have acknowledged before that the service is trailing behind the Air Force and Marines.

Just this year there has been a flurry of new activity on the Navy CCA front publicly, with several contracting notices signaling that the service’s vision for future carrier-based drones has been evolving rapidly. In August, Naval Air Systems Command (NAVAIR) notably laid out a new set of requirements more in line with an advanced uncrewed combat air vehicle (UCAV). This has been even more interesting to consider given that the Navy looked to be right on the cusp of fielding a carrier-based UCAV in the mid-2010s.

The Navy extensively flight-tested two X-47B UCAV demonstrators under its Unmanned Carrier-Launched Airborne Surveillance and Strike (UCLASS) program, including demonstrations of their ability to operate from carriers and refuel in flight. However, the service completely changed course and decided to pursue a tanker drone instead, which led to the MQ-25. The Navy’s future CCA fleets could ultimately incorporate multiple tiers of designs.

The Navy is also now investing heavily in Shield AI’s X-BAT jet-powered stealth ‘fighter’ drone with a clear eye toward fielding a version operationally. That work is currently being done through the Runway Independent Maritime Expeditionary Strike (RIMES) program, which is separate from the Navy’s CCA efforts.

X-BAT is designed to take off and land vertically from a tail-sitting position, a highly ambitious concept that could open up a host of new possibilities for employment from any ship with sufficient deck space, as well as sites on land. It is also intended to be larger and more capable than typical CCA-type drones like the ones the Air Force and Marines are pursuing now.

It remains unclear when the Navy might be looking to have its first CCAs enter operational service. Toti did say yesterday that carrier-based CCAs could begin arriving before F/A-XX, which the service hopes to see flying for carrier decks in the early 2030s.

There are separate questions already about the F/A-XX program schedule amid continued concerns about available industrial base capacity. Boeing’s defense division has been working to expand its physical production facilities to meet growing demands, including from F-47. It has also struggled with delays and cost overruns on several programs for the U.S. military, including the F-15EX Eagle II fighter, T-7A Red Hawk jet trainer, and KC-46 tanker.

“The same company that’s building F-47 is going to build the F/A-XX, and with that, we’re able to learn a lot from the Air Force to accelerate the F/A-XX program,” Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said at his own confirmation hearing earlier this week when asked about steps being taken to keep the Navy’s next-generation fighter program on track. “We literally just awarded the contract a little over a month ago. We’re doing the preliminary decisions [sic] to see how much it would cost in order to get the low-rate initial product out there, so that we can accelerate the program and get the next-generation fighter.”

Just how closely related Boeing F-47 and F/A-XX designs are remains unknown. However, TWZ has previously pointed out that Boeing will be able to leverage relevant design work, as well as production experience and supply chains, regardless.
Cao was insistent that the Navy needed F/A-XX, in general, to be able to keep ahead of potential adversaries, including China and Russia.

Toti’s remarks yesterday make clear that the Navy’s CCA plans are still solidifying. At the same time, the service is looking to press ahead with the development of these new drones as an important force multiplier for carrier air wings as they exist now.

items.titel: The Real Miami Museums and Artists Behind GTA VI’s Vice City
items.anriss: After 13 agonizing years of waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), gamers worldwide wasted no time tearing up the streets of the game's fictional state of Leonida after it was released yesterday, November 19. The South Florida-inspired …

absaetze.t: From The Bass in Miami Beach to the murals of Wynwood, the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is heavily inspired by the local arts scene.
November 20, 2026 — 4 min read

After 13 agonizing years of waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), gamers worldwide wasted no time tearing up the streets of the game's fictional state of Leonida after it was released yesterday, November 19. The South Florida-inspired game environment is heavily influenced by the culture, environment, and architecture of Miami — from its Art Deco resorts, white-sand beaches, Cuban quarter, and strip clubs, right down to its museums and arts venues.

As fans embed themselves in GTA 6's immersive landscape, many have recognized real-life locations across South Florida making unexpected cameos. One such case is the Vice Museum of Art, which Rockstar Games confirmed is modeled after the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach.

“It was totally unexpected to see Grand Theft Auto VI reimagine The Bass as the ‘Vice City Museum of Art,’” said Silvia Karman Cubiñá, executive director of the Bass Museum of Art, in an email to Hyperallergic.
“It’s a wonderful reminder of how art and architecture can become part of popular culture,” she continued. “Now, I’m just curious: will the Vice City Museum of Art get more visitors than we do?!”

While not listed as a landmark like the Vice Museum of Art, another building in Downtown Vice City appears to be directly modeled after the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). Situated near the Vice City Arts Center, which is heavily based on Miami's Adrienne Arsht Center for Performing Arts, the PAMM-inspired building sits right on the water's edge just as the museum does in real life.

“We were as delighted as anyone else to find PAMM in what feels like the biggest video game of all time,” said Alexa Ferra, PAMM's senior director of marketing and communications, in an email to Hyperallergic.
Ferra attached a photo someone sent her from the game showing the PAMM dupe and some gummy bear-inspired sculptures installed in the shallow water.
“It's a testament to our stunning Herzog & de Meuron building, and goes to show if you stick around long enough, you'll pop up in the unlikeliest — but inevitable — of places.” Ferra added.

Other references to Miami's arts and culture scene include Leonida's Stockyard neighborhood, which directly channels the street murals and warehouse-lined roads of the Wynwood Arts District. It was reported earlier this summer that Rockstar Games had hired over 50 real street artists to design the in-game murals across Stockyard. Users shared they've spotted the works of street artist Ahol Sniffs Glue (David Anasagasti), among others.

Miami-raised contemporary photographer Josh Aronson also took notice of GTA 6's inclusion of his installation at the Catalina Hotel & Beach Club in Miami Beach during Miami Art Week 2024, which Rockstar Games incorporated in Vice City's own Catalina Hotel. From Aronson's Florida Boys (2020–) photo series, the photo “Spring” (2024) was made into an enormous sublimated fabric print that hung from the second-story window of the hotel.
The same printed photo, which features a group of cheerful young men photographed from above while floating in water, is shown at Vice City's Catalina Hotel.

“Florida Boys is my own imagined version of Florida, so I love that it gets to live on in another imagined Florida,” Aronson told Hyperallergic. “The installation at the Catalina was temporary, but in Vice City, someone might stumble upon it years from now. It’s a reminder of the wild ways we encounter art today, and how a work can find new life long after it comes down.”

GTA6's pre-holiday release comes just before Miami Art Week begins early next month. Those dropping in can find some of Aronson's installations on view beyond Vice City at the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens and the Museum of Contemporary Art, North Miami, and also pay homage to the cultural venues and districts that inspired Leonida.

absaetze.t: “I love that my roommate’s cat, Astrid, whom I appointed as my studio assistant, can always come and join me when I am painting.”
November 20, 2026 — 3 min read

Welcome to the 364th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Rei Xiao paints a world of surreal, feline figuration into being while navigating the artist visa system and managing their studio assistant (a dignified cat named Astrid).
Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.
Rei Xiao, Brooklyn, New York
How long have you been working in this space?
Two years.
Describe an average day in your studio.

I work from my apartment. The most predictable parts of my studio day start with putting on my sunscreen and painting clothes. It’s a very small space that I paint in, so I usually have to push stuff aside when I start, like my painting cart, stool, and trash bin.

I, then, turn on my air purifier, open the lids of my palettes, scrape paints from the previous session, and play either TV shows I’m familiar with or podcasts hosted by comedians in the background. The day usually ends with my cleaning the palette, emptying and wiping my brush cleaning tank, and diligently washing my brushes. Then I wash my face and go to sleep.

items.titel: « Il ne suffit pas d’être érudit, encore faut-il le montrer » : le raffinement des élites de l’ancienne Corée révélé dans 2 expositions à Paris
items.anriss: En Corée , durant l’ère Joseon (1392-1910), il ne suffit pas d’être érudit pour passer pour un lettré, encore faut-il le montrer. Hanter les bibliothèques, pourquoi pas, du moment qu’elles sont visibles en tant que marqueur de rang, …

absaetze.t: En Corée, durant l’ère Joseon (1392-1910), il ne suffit pas d’être érudit pour passer pour un lettré, encore faut-il le montrer. Hanter les bibliothèques, pourquoi pas, du moment qu’elles sont visibles en tant que marqueur de rang, instrument de pouvoir et idéal moral – quitte à n’être qu’un trompe l’œil. Les deux musées parisiens dessinent cet hiver le portait de l’élite yangban, qui se met en scène à travers son décor, entre autorité intellectuelle et austérité raffiné.
L’art du trompe-l’œil

Ce paravent représentant une bibliothèque est sans doute l’un des témoignages les plus proches des premiers chaekgado (« peintures à étagères compartimentées »), commandes du roi Jeongjo à la fin du XVIIIe siècle, dont les prototypes ne sont pas conservés. L’installation d’un grand nombre de ces bibliothèques en trompe-l’œil dans le palais de Changdeok plaçait symboliquement l’étude dans l’orbite du souverain, présentant le monarque comme le gardien du savoir légitime.

Paravent à dix panneaux représentant une bibliothèque, époque du Joseon, xixe-xxe siècle, encre et couleurs sur soie, 206,5 x 453 cm, détail, Séoul, musée national du Palais de Corée. ©licence KOGL. Exposé au musée Guimet.
Le lettré mis en scène

Les portraits officiels de la période Joseon (1392-1910) relèvent autant de la description d’une individualité que d’un moyen d’affirmation du statut politique, de l’autorité intellectuelle et des idéaux moraux des yangban, les lettrés coréens. Yi Ki-ji (1690-1722), connu pour avoir rédigé l’Ilam yŏn’gi, récit de son voyage à Pékin, pose assis sur un siège de cérémonie, coiffé d’un chapeau et vêtu d’un costume de lettré.
Portrait de Yi Ki-Ji, 1718, encre et couleurs sur soie, 116 x 56,5 cm, détail, Séoul, musée de l’Université de Corée. Exposé au musée Cernuschi.
Équilibre et harmonie

Ce bel éventail aux nuances orangées est orné d’un taegeuk, la version coréenne du yin-yang, symbole d’équilibre et d’harmonie. Il fait partie des objets que les peintres de la période Joseon aimaient représenter dans les chaekgeori, ces peintures représentant des livres et des objets de savoir, qui pouvaient être en trompe-l’œil ou sous forme de natures mortes. L’éventail servait alors à marquer la distance entre le premier et le second plan.
Éventail à motif de tægeuk, époque du Joseon, XIXe siècle, bois et papier, 84 x 43 x 2,5 cm, Paris, musée Guimet. ©Presse GrandPalaisRMN. Exposé au musée Guimet.
Décor pour lettré

Les paravents de bureau étaient toujours à la mode au début du XXe siècle en Corée. Sur celui-ci figurent des livres et des objets (vases, théières…) dont les contours ont été peints de diverses couleurs pour éviter une monochromie monotone. Y apparaissent des fruits et des légumes de bon augure – cédrats digités, pêches, radis et maïs-, ainsi que des fleurs très appréciées des lettrés.
Paravent de bureau à douze panneaux, 1918, encre, couleurs et or sur soie, 185,2 x 436,8 cm, détail, Séoul, musée national de Corée. ©licence KOGL. Exposé au musée Guimet.
Simplicité et raffinement

Alliant fonctionnalité et esthétique, ce cabinet pour pierre à encre, témoin matériel des activités intellectuelles des lettrés, se caractérise par des formes austères mettant en valeur le grain du bois, et par le raffinement de son assemblage. Le compartiment abritant la pierre à encre et le compte-goutte en céramique se situe dans la partie supérieure, soutenue par une base ouverte dont la forme des moulures rappelle des fenêtres.
Cabinet pour pierre à encre, XIXe siècle, ginkgo, 17,8 x 20 x 40 cm, Séoul, musée de l’Université de Corée. Exposé au musée Cernuschi.
Noblesse de robe

Les fonctionnaires lettrés du Joseon devaient, dans l’exercice de leur charge, porter une coiffe à ailettes, une robe, une ceinture autour de la taille et des bottines. Le statut de cette élite dirigeante reposait à la fois sur son lignage et la réussite aux examens (gwageo) qui sanctionnaient principalement la maîtrise des textes classiques confucéens, afin de seconder le souverain et d’administrer le pays.
Robe de fonctionnaire, fin de la période Joseon, xixe siècle, soie, 138 x 182 cm, détail, Séoul, musée de l’Université de Corée. Exposée au musée Cernuschi.
Broderies de haut rang

La pièce de tissu brodée (hyungbae) ornant la poitrine et le dos de la robe des fonctionnaires constituait un marqueur de rang explicite. À partir de 1734, les robes des fonctionnaires civils étaient reconnaissables à leur décor de grues tandis que les fonctionnaires militaires arboraient des tigres, des léopards ou des ours. Les doubles grues et doubles tigres étaient réservés aux fonctionnaires de rang supérieur.
Insigne de poitrine de fonctionnaire orné de deux tigres, xixe siècle, soie, 26,5 x 25,4 cm, Séoul, musée de l’Université de Corée. Exposée au musée Cernuschi.
La terre, le feu et l’esprit

À la différence des céramiques émaillées roses et jaunes propres aux créations chinoises, les porcelaines monochromes lustrées, comme cette théière à la teinte verte tirant vers le bleu, sont une fabrication propre aux goûts des hautes classes du Joseon. Elles offraient un apaisement pour la vue et le toucher, inspiraient l’élévation intellectuelle. Elles figurent souvent dans les bibliothèques imaginaires peintes de type chaekgeori.
Théière, époque du Joseon, XIXe siècle, porcelaine à couverte lavande, 10,5 x 15 cm, Paris, musée Guimet. ©Presse GrandPalaisRMN. Exposée au musée Guimet.

items.titel: National Gallery of Canada receives major gift of modern and contemporary glass art
items.anriss: A promised donation of 56 glass works from the Bronfman family, accompanied by an endowment for a new curatorial position, marks a significant expansion of the museum’s decorative arts holdings

absaetze.t: The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a new chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman. Accompanied by an endowment to establish the institution’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design, the donation will help broaden the museum’s collection and increase its scholarly contributions.

“This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper. “It significantly expands our understanding of art history, bringing together artistic expression and material and technical innovation.”

The gifted Bronfman Collection spans more than a century of glass experimentation, with works by 29 artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia. The collection traces the medium’s evolution from the sinuous forms of Art Nouveau and Arts and Crafts to the streamlined aesthetics of Art Deco and Modernism. Early 20th-century examples by Tiffany Studios, Émile Gallé and the renowned studio Daum demonstrate how artists pushed glass beyond traditional decorative applications.

The works also chart the emergence of studio glass as an independent discipline in the post-war period. Additional artists with works in the donation include Dale Chihuly, whose gravity-defying installations are in museums worldwide, as well as the studio glass pioneer Toots Zynsky and the well-known Canadian American artist Laura Donefer.

A selection of pieces from the collection is currently on view in the NGC’s European galleries (until 30 April 2027). Highlights of the installation include Edward Hald’s The Fireworks Bowl (around 1921), alongside architectural works by Tiffany and Frank Lloyd Wright.

“Harvey Littleton’s Red Crossed Form (1990) is another notable work that reflects the development of studio glass as an independent artistic medium,” says Anabelle Kienle Ponka, the NGC’s senior curator of European, American and Asian Art. “The presentation brings together very different approaches to glass, from the decorative traditions of the early 20th century to the formal and technical experimentation of contemporary artists.”

The international scope of the donation highlights the exchange of technical traditions, particularly the influence of Venetian glassmaking on successive generations of artists, Kienle Ponka says. Together, the works demonstrate the medium’s versatility across sculpture, architecture and ornamentation.

Equally significant for the NGC is the accompanying endowment, which will fund the museum’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design. The NGC has not shared the sum of the endowment, but notes that the post will support research, exhibitions and future acquisitions, establishing a foundation for sustained institutional engagement with the field.

“[The donation’s] significance extends well beyond this gift,” Bélisle says. “The position will allow us to pursue further acquisitions, develop exhibitions and scholarship, and build relationships with artists and institutions.”

The donation builds on a long history of the Bronfman family’s philanthropy in Canada's cultural sector. “My late wife Andy and I were admirers of the art of glass making and wanted to share this love with other Canadians,” Charles Bronfman said in a statement. “With the planned celebrations marking the upcoming 100th birthday of my sister, Phyllis Lambert, founder of the Canadian Centre for Architecture, and the 50th anniversary of the Canada Council for the Arts’ Saidye Bronfman Award, named after my mother, I am truly delighted to be contributing in this meaningful way to the national collections.”

The NGC has received other transformative gifts in recent years, including a 2025 donation of 61 contemporary works valued at C$22.8m ($16.8m) from collector Bob Rennie and his family. “The Bronfman gift is significant in a different way,” Bélisle says. “Its importance lies not only in the quality and range of the works, but also in the accompanying endowment, which will provide the expertise and resources to develop decorative arts and design as a sustained area of collecting and scholarship.”
